questions.q: What is the result of applying S to the basis state |1⟩?
questions.explain: S = diag(1, i), so multiplying by |1⟩ = [0,1]ᵀ gives [0, i]ᵀ, i.e. S|1⟩ = i|1⟩, confirmed by direct matrix-vector multiplication representing i as the pair [0,1]. The amplitude's magnitude is unchanged; only its phase angle moves.

questions.q: After computing S|1⟩ = i|1⟩, what is the measurement probability of outcome 1, and why?
options: 1, because |i|² = 1, exactly the same magnitude-squared as before S was applied
It cannot be determined without measuring
questions.explain: Measurement probability depends only on |amplitude|². Since |i|² = 1² (computed directly), the probability of measuring 1 is still exactly 1, identical to before S was applied. This is the core property of phase gates: they rotate phase without touching probabilities on a basis state alone.

questions.q: Direct matrix multiplication (S × S) produces which gate's matrix exactly?
questions.explain: Multiplying S=[[1,0],[0,i]] by itself gives [[1,0],[0,i²]] = [[1,0],[0,-1]], which is exactly the Z matrix. This confirms S² = Z — two applications of S produce the same half-turn phase flip as one application of Z.

questions.q: Based on the chain T² = S, T⁴ = Z, T⁸ = I, how many applications of T bring a qubit's phase all the way back to its starting point?
questions.explain: T applies a 45° phase step. Direct matrix multiplication confirms T⁴ = Z (a 180° half-turn) and squaring that again, T⁸, returns the identity matrix — a full 360° turn. This is why T is informally called an 'eighth-turn' gate.

questions.q: Why are S and T never used alone on a basis state in a real circuit, despite being essential gates?
options: Because they are not unitary and would violate normalization
Because applied to a basis state alone, they only change phase, which has no effect on measurement probability until that qubit is combined with an interference step like Hadamard
Because S and T can only be applied to two-qubit states, never single qubits
Because they are physically impossible to implement in real hardware
questions.explain: A phase gate applied to a pure basis state changes the complex angle of that amplitude but not its magnitude, so |amplitude|² — and therefore measurement probability — is unchanged. Their effect only becomes observable once a gate like H turns that phase difference into a measurable amplitude/probability difference, which is why phase gates are always paired with interference steps in real circuits.
